obtained.how: the University of Maryland's institutional repository DRUM (handle 1903/20202): the thesis PDF (189 pages, text layer), fetched through the repository's own bitstream link

bibliography.checked_against: the thesis title page (PDF p. 3) and abstract page
bibliography.note: Christopher James Heyer, 'Understanding maternal effects as a recruitment mechanism in Lake Michigan yellow perch (Perca flavescens)', MS thesis, University of Maryland at College Park, 2000 (advisor T. J. Miller)

claims.claim: yellow perch starved from hatch reached 50 % mortality 2.7–6.3 days after hatching
claims.location: p. 71 (PDF p. 84), Chapter 3 Results; Table 4 (Table 3.4), PDF p. 101 (raw text)
claims.quote: Line6 were the most resistant to starvation, reaching 50% mortality by 6.3 ± 0.58 days
claims.conditions: Lake Michigan yellow perch (adults caught off Milwaukee, 2 and 4 June 1998), ten maternal lines, larvae never fed from hatch, three tanks per line (n = 3), ~2,000 eggs per tank; means per line from 2.7 ± 0.58 (line 3) to 6.3 ± 0.58 dph (line 6); 10–54 % alive at 6 dph; larvae 5.7–6.3 mm TL at 50 % mortality

claims.claim: maternal lines differed twofold in resistance to starvation
claims.quote: Maternal effects resulted in a twofold difference in resistance to starvation among the maternal lines
claims.conditions: the ten lines above; resistance rose with yolk volume and fell with length at hatch
claims.note: the line means span 2.7 to 6.3 d (2.3-fold); the thesis calls it 'a factor of two'

claims.claim: at an inferred 14–16 °C (the thesis gives no temperature; the paper infers it)
claims.quote: Hatching began on 14 June 1998 in all tanks.
claims.conditions: eggs fertilised in the field on 2 and 4 June 1998 and incubated in 'flow-through, temperature-controlled' aquaria whose temperature was 'consistent with successful yellow perch rearing conditions' at the WATER Institute — no value is given anywhere in the thesis
claims.note: the source supports only the inputs of the inference: no rearing temperature is stated, and incubation lasted 10–12 days (fertilised 2/4 June, hatching from 14 June). The step from 10–12 days to 14–16 °C uses an incubation–temperature relation from elsewhere, not checked here; the paper rightly labels it 'inferred'

notes: Other values: under high food (Chapter 4), maternal effects persisted to 32 dph with threefold differences in survival among lines; RNA:DNA at 50 % mortality varied little among lines (1.1–1.26); hatchlings differed among mothers in total length, yolk volume, dry weight and DNA; Letcher et al. 1996 (cited here, p. 65) give ~6 d to 50 % mortality after feeding stopped for perch fed to 10 mm. These are hatchery larvae starved from hatch; they show how fast unfed first feeders die, not field starvation rates.
